Do you need a game data analyst? And what parts can be automated
Tomas Hubka
Last updated: Oct 15, 2026
min read
Regardless of what your role is, it’s likely you’ve recently asked yourself whether AI could replace you or how your work will change.
For game data analysts, the question seems especially pointed. Most of the day-to-day work has become something an AI agent can do in minutes. And surely all the LinkedIn posts, the layoffs at mid-size data teams, the headlines about AI replacing 80% of analyst work can act as stressors for anyone whose role's been rapidly automated lately. (Luckily) for Data Analysts, AI is coming for the technical layer of the job. A recent
piece from Databricks
frames it well:
AI isn’t ending the analyst role; it’s restoring it to what it should have been all along.
Game data analysts were never supposed to spend their weeks running ad hoc SQL for one-off requests from the LiveOps team, rebuilding the same cohort view every time a new producer joined the project, and wrestling with raw event streams that nobody had properly modeled. They were supposed to translate questions about player behavior into decisions about the game. The mechanics of execution just got in the way, and luckily that’s the part getting automated the most.
The article puts it like this:
The analyst who only does those things is being automated. The analyst who frames business problems and drives decisions is becoming more and more valuable.
It might feel like a good chunk of your day is being handed to machines, but there’s plenty left for analysts in a studio, and it gives you the freedom to focus your expertise where it matters most. So if anything, the job is sharpening, and
deciding what matters for the game is still a human call
.
Agents are good at answering questions, but not at knowing which question to ask next about your game, your player base, your current live event, or your upcoming release. That’s the kind of judgment, product context, and studio sense that only a human can bring to the table. And equally, validating whether an insight means anything still requires a human filter. AI will confidently report correlations that are noise, artifacts of selection bias in your cohort definitions, or statistical flukes from a tiny sample during a limited-time event. And it's up to you to decide whether the pattern is real. In the coming weeks, I’ll write about why AI gives confident but wrong answers and what steps you can take to prevent this. Keep an eye on our blog so you don’t miss it.
If you’re still looking for more, think about pushing back on data requests that could mislead the team. You’re surely familiar with passionate discussions about what a metric represents and how it should be interpreted. An agent can build the retention chart your CEO asked for, but your role is to flag that the chart answers the wrong question and to suggest the right methodology. The ownership of metric definitions remains yours, and when those definitions drift (which they will, as new mechanics ship and old metrics stop meaning what they used to), someone needs to catch it before the next board update is built on numbers that look right but aren’t.
And finally, qualitative context from outside the data is almost entirely human. Think App Store policy changes affecting reward video placement, or a competitor shipping a feature that pulled your audience’s attention for two weeks. The warehouse doesn’t know about any of that, but you (ideally) do.
This thread, which went around a few weeks ago, captures the practical version of my point and the role's shift well:
@ezekiel_aleke If the exec suite can just ask for a dashboard now. That means it’s even more crucial to get the setup done right.
Process. Business rules. Definitions. Ownership. Data products and models.
